items.stem: What is a magnetic field?
options: a region in which a stationary charge experiences a force
a region in which a magnetic pole, a moving charge or a current-carrying conductor experiences a force
a region in which a mass experiences a force
the space inside a magnet only
items.answer: a region in which a magnetic pole, a moving charge or a current-carrying conductor experiences a force
items.markingKey: Definition of magnetic field.

items.stem: Describe the magnetic field pattern of a flat circular coil carrying a current.
items.answer: Near the wire the lines are circles around it; at the centre of the coil the lines are straight, perpendicular to the plane of the coil; the pattern is like that of a short bar magnet.
items.markingKey: circles round each side of wire [1]; straight through the centre perpendicular to coil [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why two parallel wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel.
items.answer: Each wire is in the magnetic field of the other; by Fleming's left-hand rule the force on each wire is directed away from the other, so they repel (equal and opposite forces, N3).
items.markingKey: each wire in the other's field [1]; FLHR gives forces apart [1] [2]

items.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a current vertically upwards. Freya places a plotting compass on a horizontal card a short distance to the south of the wire (ignore the Earth's field). In which direction does the north end of the compass point?
items.answer: towards the east
items.markingKey: Right-hand grip rule: viewed from above the field is anticlockwise; at the south side it points east.

items.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a current vertically upwards. Use the right-hand grip rule to state the direction of the magnetic field at a point a short distance to the west of the wire, and describe the shape of the field lines.
items.answer: Towards the south; concentric circles around the wire (anticlockwise viewed from above)
items.markingKey: direction south [1]; concentric circles, sense correct [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya investigates the magnetic field of a long solenoid carrying a current of 3.0 A in a laboratory in Doha. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (b) Explain why a plotting compass placed inside near the centre lines up along the axis. (c) Describe the force between two adjacent turns of the coil.
items.answer: (a) Inside: uniform, parallel to the axis. Outside: like a bar magnet, lines from N end round to S end. (b) The field there is parallel to the axis, and the compass aligns with the field. (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract.
items.markingKey: (a) inside uniform [1]; outside bar-magnet pattern [1] [2] (b) The field there is parallel to the axis, and the compass aligns with the field [1] (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract [1]

items.stem: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire?
options: concentric circles centred on the wire
straight lines parallel to the wire
items.answer: concentric circles centred on the wire
items.markingKey: Field lines are circles in planes perpendicular to the wire.

items.stem: Explain why the field outside a long solenoid is much weaker than inside.
items.answer: Inside, the fields of all turns add along the axis, concentrated in a small area; outside, the same lines spread out over a very large region, so the flux density is small.
items.markingKey: fields of turns add inside [1]; lines spread out outside [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how iron filings and a plotting compass can be used to show the field pattern of a current-carrying wire.
items.answer: Pass the wire vertically through a horizontal card; sprinkle filings and tap: they line up in concentric circles. A plotting compass placed on the card shows the direction of the field at each point (the N end points along the field).
items.markingKey: filings show shape of lines [1]; compass shows direction [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern of a flat circular coil carrying a current. (b) Explain why the field outside a long solenoid is much weaker than inside.
items.answer: (a) Near the wire the lines are circles around it; at the centre of the coil the lines are straight, perpendicular to the plane of the coil; the pattern is like that of a short bar magnet. (b) Inside, the fields of all turns add along the axis, concentrated in a small area; outside, the same lines spread out over a very large region, so the flux density is small.
items.markingKey: (a) circles round each side of wire [1]; straight through the centre perpendicular to coil [1] [2] (b) fields of turns add inside [1]; lines spread out outside [1] [2]

items.stem: A solenoid lies horizontally. Viewed from its left-hand end, the current flows clockwise. The left-hand end of the solenoid behaves as
options: a north pole and a south pole alternately
not a pole, the field there is zero
items.answer: a south pole
items.markingKey: Viewed from an end: clockwise current gives a S pole, anticlockwise gives a N pole. Here: south.

items.stem: A horizontal solenoid carries a current that flows clockwise when viewed from its left-hand end. State which pole is formed at the left-hand end, describe the field inside the solenoid, and state what happens to the poles if the current is reversed.
items.answer: South pole at the left-hand end; uniform field parallel to the axis inside; reversing the current swaps the poles.
items.markingKey: south pole [1]; uniform, parallel to axis [1]; poles reverse [1] [3]

items.stem: Kwame investigates the magnetic field of a long solenoid carrying a current of 3.0 A in a laboratory in Cape Town. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (b) Explain how to identify which end is the north pole. (c) Explain why a plotting compass placed inside near the centre lines up along the axis.
items.answer: (a) Inside: uniform, parallel to the axis. Outside: like a bar magnet, lines from N end round to S end. (b) Right-hand grip rule: fingers in the direction of the current, thumb points to the N pole (or view from the end: anticlockwise = N). (c) The field there is parallel to the axis, and the compass aligns with the field.
items.markingKey: (a) inside uniform [1]; outside bar-magnet pattern [1] [2] (b) Right-hand grip rule: fingers in the direction of the current, thumb points to the N pole (or view from the end: anticlockwise = N) [1] (c) The field there is parallel to the axis, and the compass aligns with the field [1]

items.stem: Hana investigates the magnetic field of a long solenoid carrying a current of 5.0 A in a laboratory in Cairo. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (b) State two ways to increase the field strength. (c) Describe the force between two adjacent turns of the coil.
items.answer: (a) Inside: uniform, parallel to the axis. Outside: like a bar magnet, lines from N end round to S end. (b) Increase the current; increase turns per unit length; insert an iron core. (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract.
items.markingKey: (a) inside uniform [1]; outside bar-magnet pattern [1] [2] (b) first way [1]; second way [1] [2] (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract [1]

items.stem: Which is the definition of the tesla?
options: the field produced by 1 A in a 1 m wire
the field that induces 1 V in a 1 m wire
the uniform flux density that produces a force of 1 N on a 1 m length of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field
the flux through an area of 1 m²
items.answer: the uniform flux density that produces a force of 1 N on a 1 m length of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field
items.markingKey: B = F/(IL) with θ = 90°.

items.stem: Explain why a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force.
items.answer: The current produces its own magnetic field around the wire, which interacts with the external field (stronger on one side, weaker on the other), giving a resultant force; equivalently, each moving charge experiences a force BQv.
items.markingKey: interaction of fields / force on moving charges [1]; perpendicular to both B and I [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how a current balance can be used to measure magnetic flux density.
items.answer: A wire frame of length L in the field is balanced; when a current I flows, the force BIL tips it; add a rider of known mass m to rebalance (or measure on a top-pan balance): BIL = mg, so B = mg/(IL).
items.markingKey: force measured via balance/mass [1]; B = F/(IL) [1] [2]

items.stem: A straight wire of length 10 cm in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.60 T carries a current of 1.5 A at 90° to the field. Calculate the force on the wire.
items.markingKey: F = BIL sin θ = 0.60 × 1.5 × 0.10 × sin 90° = 0.090 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A straight wire of length 5.0 cm in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.080 T carries a current of 6.0 A at 90° to the field. Calculate the force on the wire and state the angle for which the force would be zero.
items.answer: 0.024 N; 0° (parallel to the field)
items.markingKey: F = BIL sin θ [1]; = 0.024 N [1]; zero when parallel [1] [3]

items.stem: A horizontal copper rod of mass 2.0 g and length 8.0 cm lies at right angles to a horizontal uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.40 T. (a) Calculate the current needed for the magnetic force to support the weight of the rod. (b) State how the direction of the current must be chosen. (c) Calculate the force on the rod if the current is 3.0 A and the rod is turned to 30° to the field.
items.answer: (a) 0.613 A (b) so that Fleming's left-hand rule gives an upward force (c) 0.048 N
items.markingKey: (a) BIL = mg [1]; I = 0.613 A [1] (b) FLHR, force upwards [1] (c) F = BIL sin θ [1]; = 0.048 N [1] [5]

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 100 turns, with sides 5.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 3.0 cm, carries a current of 0.20 A. Its plane is parallel to a uniform field of flux density 0.30 T. (a) Define the tesla. (b) Calculate the torque on the coil. (c) State the force on the sides parallel to the field.
items.answer: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field. (b) 0.00900 N m (c) Zero (sin 0° = 0).
items.markingKey: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field [1] (b) torque = F × separation (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.00900 N m with unit [1] [2] (c) Zero (sin 0° = 0) [1]

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 200 turns, with sides 5.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 3.0 cm, carries a current of 0.50 A. Its plane is parallel to a uniform field of flux density 0.20 T. (a) Define the tesla. (b) Calculate the force on one of the sides perpendicular to the field. (c) Calculate the torque on the coil.
items.answer: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field. (b) 1.0 N (c) 0.030 N m
items.markingKey: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field [1] (b) F = NBIL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.0 N with unit [1] [2] (c) torque = F × separation (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.030 N m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A wire of length 0.20 m carries 3.0 A at right angles to a field of 0.50 T. What is the force on it?
A current-carrying wire is parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The force on it is …
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: F = BIL sin θ, θ = 0.

items.stem: Explain why the force on a wire is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field.
items.answer: F = BIL sin θ; sin θ has its maximum value 1 when θ = 90°, so the whole current is perpendicular to B.
items.markingKey: F ∝ sin θ [1]; maximum at 90° [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a rectangular coil carrying a current in a uniform field experiences a turning effect but no resultant force.
items.answer: Opposite sides carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them are equal and opposite (no resultant force) but act along different lines, forming a couple.
items.markingKey: equal and opposite forces on opposite sides [1]; not in line → couple / torque [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a rectangular coil carrying a current in a uniform field experiences a turning effect but no resultant force. (b) Describe how a current balance can be used to measure magnetic flux density.
items.answer: (a) Opposite sides carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them are equal and opposite (no resultant force) but act along different lines, forming a couple. (b) A wire frame of length L in the field is balanced; when a current I flows, the force BIL tips it; add a rider of known mass m to rebalance (or measure on a top-pan balance): BIL = mg, so B = mg/(IL).
items.markingKey: (a) equal and opposite forces on opposite sides [1]; not in line → couple / torque [1] [2] (b) force measured via balance/mass [1]; B = F/(IL) [1] [2]

items.stem: A straight wire of length 8.0 cm in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T carries a current of 6.0 A at 30° to the field. What is the force on the wire?

A wire of length 8.0 cm is clamped horizontally between the poles of a magnet resting on a top-pan balance, at right angles to the field. As the current is increased the balance reading changes: I = 1.0 A, reading change = 0.37 g; I = 2.0 A, reading change = 0.73 g; I = 3.0 A, reading change = 1.10 g; I = 4.0 A, reading change = 1.47 g; I = 5.0 A, reading change = 1.83 g. Use the data to determine the magnetic flux density.
items.answer: gradient = 0.367 g A⁻¹ = 3.67 × 10⁻⁴ kg A⁻¹; B = gradient × g/L = 0.045 T
items.markingKey: F = Δm × g [1]; gradient of Δm against I [1]; B = g × gradient/L = 0.045 T [1] [3]

items.stem: A straight wire of length 8.0 cm in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T carries a current of 1.5 A at 45° to the field. Determine the force on the wire.
items.markingKey: F = BIL sin θ = 0.25 × 1.5 × 0.080 × sin 45° = 0.0212 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A horizontal copper rod of mass 3.0 g and length 8.0 cm lies at right angles to a horizontal uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. (a) Calculate the current needed for the magnetic force to support the weight of the rod. (b) State how the direction of the current must be chosen. (c) Calculate the force on the rod if the current is 6.0 A and the rod is turned to 45° to the field.
items.answer: (a) 7.36 A (b) so that Fleming's left-hand rule gives an upward force (c) 0.0170 N
items.markingKey: (a) BIL = mg [1]; I = 7.36 A [1] (b) FLHR, force upwards [1] (c) F = BIL sin θ [1]; = 0.0170 N [1] [5]

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 200 turns, with sides 8.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 4.0 cm, carries a current of 0.20 A. Its plane is parallel to a uniform field of flux density 0.20 T. (a) Define the tesla. (b) Calculate the force on one of the sides perpendicular to the field.
items.answer: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field. (b) 0.64 N
items.markingKey: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field [1] (b) F = NBIL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.64 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 100 turns, with sides 8.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 3.0 cm, carries a current of 0.20 A. Its plane is parallel to a uniform field of flux density 0.15 T. (a) Calculate the force on one of the sides perpendicular to the field. (b) State the force on the sides parallel to the field.
items.answer: (a) 0.24 N (b) Zero (sin 0° = 0).
items.markingKey: (a) F = NBIL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.24 N with unit [1] [2] (b) Zero (sin 0° = 0) [1]

items.stem: An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a field of 0.10 T. What is the force on it?
Explain how the Hall voltage is established across a current-carrying slice in a magnetic field.
items.answer: The charge carriers experience a force BQv perpendicular to their drift, so they accumulate on one face (and leave the opposite charge on the other). This produces an electric field across the slice; equilibrium is reached when QE = BQv, i.e. Q V_H/d = BQv.
items.markingKey: carriers deflected, build up on one side [1]; electric force balances magnetic force [1] [2]

items.stem: Derive the expression V_H = BI/(ntq) for the Hall voltage across a slice of width d and thickness t.
items.answer: At equilibrium qV_H/d = Bqv, so V_H = Bvd. With I = nAvq and A = dt, v = I/(ndtq). So V_H = BId/(ndtq) = BI/(ntq).
items.markingKey: qV_H/d = Bqv [1]; substitute v = I/(nAq) with A = dt [1] [2]

items.stem: A singly charged ion moves at 5.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T. Calculate the magnetic force on it.
items.markingKey: F = BQv sin θ = 0.50 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁵ × sin 30° = 2.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An α-particle moves at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ at 60° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T. Work out the magnetic force on it.
items.markingKey: F = BQv sin θ = 0.50 × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁷ × sin 60° = 2.77 × 10⁻¹² N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A Hall probe slice of width 5.0 mm and thickness 0.20 mm contains 1.5 × 10²¹ free electrons per m³. It carries a current of 20 mA and is placed perpendicular to a field of 0.30 T. (a) Calculate the drift speed of the electrons. (b) Explain why the Hall voltage reaches a steady value.
items.answer: (a) 83.3 m s⁻¹ (b) Charge builds up on one side until the electric force eV_H/d equals the magnetic force Bev.
items.markingKey: (a) v = I/(nAq), A = dt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 83.3 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) charge accumulates on one face [1]; electric force eV_H/d balances Bev [1] [2]

items.stem: The magnetic force on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field is always …
items.answer: perpendicular to its velocity
items.markingKey: F = BQv sin θ, perpendicular to v and B.

items.stem: Explain why the magnetic force on a moving charged particle does no work.
items.answer: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so there is no displacement in the direction of the force; the kinetic energy (speed) is unchanged.
items.markingKey: force ⊥ velocity [1]; no work, speed constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why Hall probes are made from semiconductors rather than metals.
items.answer: Semiconductors have a much smaller n, so V_H = BI/(ntq) is much larger and easier to measure for a given B and I.
items.markingKey: smaller n [1]; larger, measurable Hall voltage [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a Hall probe must be oriented to measure the flux density of a field.
items.answer: The probe face must be perpendicular to the field lines (field perpendicular to the current in the slice), so that the full BQv acts; rotate until the Hall voltage is maximum.
items.markingKey: field perpendicular to slice / current [1]; maximum reading [1] [2]

items.stem: A Hall probe uses a slice of copper of thickness 1.0 mm with 8.5 × 10²⁸ charge carriers per m³ (charge e). A current of 2.0 A flows in the slice, which is perpendicular to a field of 0.40 T. Calculate the Hall voltage.
items.markingKey: V_H = BI/(ntq) = 0.40 × 2.0/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.00 × 10⁻³ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.88 × 10⁻⁸ V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A Hall probe uses a slice of n-type silicon of thickness 1.0 mm with 1.0 × 10²¹ charge carriers per m³ (charge e). A current of 0.010 A flows in the slice, which is perpendicular to a field of 0.20 T. Calculate the Hall voltage and state how it changes if the current is doubled.
items.answer: 1.25 × 10⁻² V; doubles
items.markingKey: V_H = BI/(ntq) [1]; = 1.25 × 10⁻² V [1]; V_H ∝ I so doubles [1] [3]

items.stem: A Hall probe slice of width 5.0 mm and thickness 0.20 mm contains 3.0 × 10²¹ free electrons per m³. It carries a current of 20 mA and is placed perpendicular to a field of 0.30 T. (a) Calculate the drift speed of the electrons. (b) Calculate the Hall voltage.
items.markingKey: (a) v = I/(nAq), A = dt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 41.7 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) V_H = BI/(ntq) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.25 × 10⁻² V [1] [2]

items.stem: A Hall probe slice of width 5.0 mm and thickness 0.20 mm contains 3.0 × 10²¹ free electrons per m³. It carries a current of 40 mA and is placed perpendicular to a field of 0.30 T. (a) Calculate the drift speed of the electrons. (b) Explain why the Hall voltage reaches a steady value. (c) State how the probe could be used to show that a field is uniform.
items.answer: (a) 83.3 m s⁻¹ (b) Charge builds up on one side until the electric force eV_H/d equals the magnetic force Bev. (c) Move it to different positions with the same orientation; the Hall voltage stays the same.
items.markingKey: (a) v = I/(nAq), A = dt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 83.3 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) charge accumulates on one face [1]; electric force eV_H/d balances Bev [1] [2] (c) Move it to different positions with the same orientation; the Hall voltage stays the same [1]

items.stem: In a velocity selector, particles pass undeflected when their speed v satisfies …
items.answer: v = E/B
items.markingKey: eE = Bev ⇒ v = E/B.

items.stem: Explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle.
items.answer: The magnetic force Bqv has constant magnitude (speed constant) and is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it provides a centripetal force: Bqv = mv²/r with r constant.
items.markingKey: force constant magnitude ⊥ v [1]; acts as centripetal force [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the speed selected by a velocity selector does not depend on the mass or charge of the particles.
items.answer: qE = Bqv: the charge cancels and mass does not appear, so v = E/B for any particle.
items.markingKey: q cancels [1]; no mass term [1] [2]

items.stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of strength 8.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. Calculate the speed of the particles that pass through undeflected.
items.markingKey: qE = Bqv ⇒ v = E/B = 8.0 × 10⁴/0.050 = 1.60 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of strength 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. The electric field is produced by plates 1.0 cm apart. Calculate the speed selected and the p.d. between the plates.

In a mass spectrometer, singly charged neon ions pass through a velocity selector (E = 2.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, B = 0.20 T) and then enter a region with only a magnetic field of 0.50 T, where they travel in semicircles. (a) Calculate the speed of ions leaving the velocity selector. (b) Explain why the ions must all have the same speed. (c) Explain why the ions do not gain kinetic energy in the magnetic field.
items.answer: (a) 1.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (b) r depends on both m and v; with v fixed, r ∝ m so position identifies mass. (c) The magnetic force is perpendicular to their velocity, so it does no work.
items.markingKey: (a) v = E/B (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) r depends on both m and v; with v fixed, r ∝ m so position identifies mass [1] (c) The magnetic force is perpendicular to their velocity, so it does no work [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the condition for a charged particle to pass undeflected through crossed electric and magnetic fields. (b) A beam of particles enters a velocity selector. Particles that are faster than E/B are …
items.answer: (a) The electric force equals the magnetic force in magnitude and is opposite in direction: qE = Bqv, so v = E/B. (b) deflected in the direction of the magnetic force
items.markingKey: (a) qE = Bqv [1] (b) Bqv > qE for larger v.

items.stem: Explain how the specific charge e/mₑ of the electron can be found by deflecting an electron beam in a magnetic field.
items.answer: Accelerate electrons through p.d. V: ½mv² = eV. In field B they move in a circle of measured radius r: Bev = mv²/r. Eliminating v gives e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
items.markingKey: energy equation [1]; circular motion and eliminate v [1] [2]

items.stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of strength 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. What is the speed of the particles that pass through undeflected?
An electron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.0010 T. Work out the radius of its circular path.
items.markingKey: Bqv = mv²/r ⇒ r = mv/(Bq) = 0.0569 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of strength 8.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.020 T. Work out the speed of the particles that pass through undeflected.
items.markingKey: qE = Bqv ⇒ v = E/B = 8.0 × 10⁴/0.020 = 4.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A deuteron (mass 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the radius of its path and the time for one revolution.

In a mass spectrometer, singly charged neon ions pass through a velocity selector (E = 4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, B = 0.20 T) and then enter a region with only a magnetic field of 0.25 T, where they travel in semicircles. (a) Calculate the speed of ions leaving the velocity selector. (b) Calculate the radius of the path of a neon-20 ion (mass 20u). (c) Explain why the ions must all have the same speed. (d) Explain why the ions do not gain kinetic energy in the magnetic field.
items.answer: (a) 2.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (b) 0.166 m (c) r depends on both m and v; with v fixed, r ∝ m so position identifies mass. (d) The magnetic force is perpendicular to their velocity, so it does no work.
items.markingKey: (a) v = E/B (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) r = mv/(Bq) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.166 m with unit [1] [2] (c) r depends on both m and v; with v fixed, r ∝ m so position identifies mass [1] (d) The magnetic force is perpendicular to their velocity, so it does no work [1]

items.stem: Inside a long solenoid carrying a current, the magnetic field is …
options: uniform and parallel to the axis
items.answer: uniform and parallel to the axis
items.markingKey: Parallel, equally spaced lines inside the solenoid.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the field outside a long solenoid is much weaker than inside. (b) Describe the magnetic field pattern of a flat circular coil carrying a current.
items.answer: (a) Inside, the fields of all turns add along the axis, concentrated in a small area; outside, the same lines spread out over a very large region, so the flux density is small. (b) Near the wire the lines are circles around it; at the centre of the coil the lines are straight, perpendicular to the plane of the coil; the pattern is like that of a short bar magnet.

items.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a current vertically upwards. Lucas places a plotting compass on a horizontal card a short distance to the east of the wire (ignore the Earth's field). In which direction does the north end of the compass point?
items.answer: towards the north

items.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a current vertically downwards. Use the right-hand grip rule to state the direction of the magnetic field at a point a short distance to the north of the wire, and describe the shape of the field lines.
items.answer: Towards the east; concentric circles around the wire (clockwise viewed from above)
items.markingKey: direction east [1]; concentric circles, sense correct [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara investigates the magnetic field of a long solenoid carrying a current of 2.0 A in a laboratory in Madrid. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (b) State two ways to increase the field strength. (c) Describe the force between two adjacent turns of the coil.
items.answer: (a) Inside: uniform, parallel to the axis. Outside: like a bar magnet, lines from N end round to S end. (b) Increase the current; increase turns per unit length; insert an iron core. (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract.
items.markingKey: (a) inside uniform [1]; outside bar-magnet pattern [1] [2] (b) first way [1]; second way [1] [2] (c) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract [1]

items.stem: Which rule gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
items.answer: Fleming's left-hand rule
items.markingKey: First finger field, second finger current, thumb motion (force).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe how a current balance can be used to measure magnetic flux density. (b) Explain why a rectangular coil carrying a current in a uniform field experiences a turning effect but no resultant force.
items.answer: (a) A wire frame of length L in the field is balanced; when a current I flows, the force BIL tips it; add a rider of known mass m to rebalance (or measure on a top-pan balance): BIL = mg, so B = mg/(IL). (b) Opposite sides carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them are equal and opposite (no resultant force) but act along different lines, forming a couple.
items.markingKey: (a) force measured via balance/mass [1]; B = F/(IL) [1] [2] (b) equal and opposite forces on opposite sides [1]; not in line → couple / torque [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force. (b) Describe how a current balance can be used to measure magnetic flux density.
items.answer: (a) The current produces its own magnetic field around the wire, which interacts with the external field (stronger on one side, weaker on the other), giving a resultant force; equivalently, each moving charge experiences a force BQv. (b) A wire frame of length L in the field is balanced; when a current I flows, the force BIL tips it; add a rider of known mass m to rebalance (or measure on a top-pan balance): BIL = mg, so B = mg/(IL).
items.markingKey: (a) interaction of fields / force on moving charges [1]; perpendicular to both B and I [1] [2] (b) force measured via balance/mass [1]; B = F/(IL) [1] [2]

items.stem: A wire of length 6.0 cm is clamped horizontally between the poles of a magnet resting on a top-pan balance, at right angles to the field. As the current is increased the balance reading changes: I = 1.0 A, reading change = 0.28 g; I = 2.0 A, reading change = 0.55 g; I = 3.0 A, reading change = 0.83 g; I = 4.0 A, reading change = 1.10 g; I = 5.0 A, reading change = 1.38 g. Use the data to determine the magnetic flux density.
items.answer: gradient = 0.275 g A⁻¹ = 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ kg A⁻¹; B = gradient × g/L = 0.045 T
items.markingKey: F = Δm × g [1]; gradient of Δm against I [1]; B = g × gradient/L = 0.045 T [1] [3]

items.stem: A straight wire of length 25 cm in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T carries a current of 6.0 A at 90° to the field. Work out the force on the wire.
items.markingKey: F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 6.0 × 0.25 × sin 90° = 0.18 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 100 turns, with sides 8.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 4.0 cm, carries a current of 0.20 A. Its plane is parallel to a uniform field of flux density 0.15 T. (a) Define the tesla. (b) Calculate the force on one of the sides perpendicular to the field. (c) State the force on the sides parallel to the field.
items.answer: (a) Flux density giving 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field. (b) 0.24 N (c) Zero (sin 0° = 0).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which change does the magnetic force on a moving charge produce? (b) In the Hall effect, the Hall voltage is produced because …
items.answer: (a) a change in direction but not speed (b) charge carriers are deflected to one side of the conductor
items.markingKey: (a) Force ⊥ velocity, so no work done. (b) BQv force pushes carriers sideways until the electric field balances it.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Derive the expression V_H = BI/(ntq) for the Hall voltage across a slice of width d and thickness t. (b) Explain how the Hall voltage is established across a current-carrying slice in a magnetic field.
items.answer: (a) At equilibrium qV_H/d = Bqv, so V_H = Bvd. With I = nAvq and A = dt, v = I/(ndtq). So V_H = BId/(ndtq) = BI/(ntq). (b) The charge carriers experience a force BQv perpendicular to their drift, so they accumulate on one face (and leave the opposite charge on the other). This produces an electric field across the slice; equilibrium is reached when QE = BQv, i.e. Q V_H/d = BQv.
items.markingKey: (a) qV_H/d = Bqv [1]; substitute v = I/(nAq) with A = dt [1] [2] (b) carriers deflected, build up on one side [1]; electric force balances magnetic force [1] [2]

items.stem: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ at 90° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Calculate the magnetic force on it.
items.markingKey: F = BQv sin θ = 0.25 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁵ × sin 90° = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An α-particle moves at 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at 60° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Calculate the magnetic force on it.
items.markingKey: F = BQv sin θ = 0.25 × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁶ × sin 60° = 2.77 × 10⁻¹³ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A Hall probe slice of width 4.0 mm and thickness 0.20 mm contains 1.5 × 10²¹ free electrons per m³. It carries a current of 40 mA and is placed perpendicular to a field of 0.30 T. (a) Calculate the magnetic force on one electron. (b) Calculate the Hall voltage. (c) Explain why the Hall voltage reaches a steady value. (d) State how the probe could be used to show that a field is uniform.
items.answer: (a) 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁷ N (b) 2.50 × 10⁻¹ V (c) Charge builds up on one side until the electric force eV_H/d equals the magnetic force Bev. (d) Move it to different positions with the same orientation; the Hall voltage stays the same.
items.markingKey: (a) F = Bev: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁷ N [1] (b) V_H = BI/(ntq) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.50 × 10⁻¹ V [1] [2] (c) charge accumulates on one face [1]; electric force eV_H/d balances Bev [1] [2] (d) Move it to different positions with the same orientation; the Hall voltage stays the same [1]

items.stem: Explain how a mass spectrometer separates isotopes.
items.answer: Ions of the same charge are selected to have the same speed (E/B); in a uniform magnetic field r = mv/(Bq), so heavier isotopes follow larger circles and arrive at different positions.
items.markingKey: same speed via selector [1]; r ∝ m in magnetic field [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how the specific charge e/mₑ of the electron can be found by deflecting an electron beam in a magnetic field. (b) Explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle.
items.answer: (a) Accelerate electrons through p.d. V: ½mv² = eV. In field B they move in a circle of measured radius r: Bev = mv²/r. Eliminating v gives e/m = 2V/(B²r²). (b) The magnetic force Bqv has constant magnitude (speed constant) and is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it provides a centripetal force: Bqv = mv²/r with r constant.
items.markingKey: (a) energy equation [1]; circular motion and eliminate v [1] [2] (b) force constant magnitude ⊥ v [1]; acts as centripetal force [1] [2]

items.stem: A deuteron (mass 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 8.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Determine the radius of its circular path.
items.markingKey: Bqv = mv²/r ⇒ r = mv/(Bq) = 0.835 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why two parallel wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel. (b) Describe the magnetic field pattern of a flat circular coil carrying a current.
items.answer: (a) Each wire is in the magnetic field of the other; by Fleming's left-hand rule the force on each wire is directed away from the other, so they repel (equal and opposite forces, N3). items.markingKey: (a) each wire in the other's field [1]; FLHR gives forces apart [1] [2] (b) circles round each side of wire [1]; straight through the centre perpendicular to coil [1] [2]

items.stem: An electromagnet used in a scrapyard in Dubai consists of a solenoid carrying 2.0 A wound on an iron core. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (c) The field there is parallel to the axis, and the compass aligns with the field. (d) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract.
